user: Why does reactive power affect voltage?

grid.name: PGLib IEEE 30-Bus System (Alsac–Stott)
grid.description: Synthetic 7-day profile generated from the bundled PGLib IEEE 30-bus (Alsac–Stott) MATPOWER case: five dispatchable units with their own costs, line ratings from PGLib.

assistant:
Reactive power affects voltage because moving it through the grid takes current, and current flowing through the grid’s impedance creates voltage changes.

A useful simplified relation for a line is:

\[
\Delta V \approx \frac{R P + X Q}{V}
\]

where \(R\) and \(X\) are the line’s resistance and reactance, and \(P\) and \(Q\) are the active and reactive power flowing through it. In transmission networks, reactance is often significant, so reactive-power flow has a strong effect on voltage magnitude.

Generally, supplying reactive power locally tends to raise voltage; absorbing it tends to lower voltage. The effect depends on where the reactive power is supplied or consumed and on the network’s impedance. It is not unlimited: generators can adjust reactive output only within their capability, and once those limits are reached they may no longer be able to hold their voltage set-point.
